stories.headline: Reka's Rho-1 puts text, video and robot control in one 19B model
stories.standfirst: Reka says its 19-billion-parameter Rho-1 draws images, edits video and outputs robot joint trajectories from one network, trained on 320 H100 GPUs. It is a research preview, and Reka lists its own limits.
body: Reka AI has announced Rho-1, a 19-billion-parameter model that Reka says "understands and generates text, images, and video, reasons over them, and takes actions" inside a single neural network. The Decoder reported the launch on 5 October. Reka calls it a research preview, and the announcement gives a contact address for partnership inquiries rather than a download or a price.

Reka says text, pixels and physical actions are all tokens in one context window, so the model needs no tool calls or helper models. In its post, Rho-1 draws images, detects objects, animates scenes and edits video in one conversation. It can also stream video that responds to live instructions, which Reka describes as "infinite, steerable livestreams".

For robots, Reka says the model treats actions as native tokens and can simulate future movements and output joint trajectories without an external planning layer. It says it extracted control signals from ordinary internet video with an inverse dynamics model, because robot training data is scarce. The Decoder says no robot types or demonstrations were detailed.

Reka puts the base model at 0.79 times real time and a distilled version at about one second per video, and says it trained on 320 H100 GPUs over about three months. The post concedes structural drift in long sequences, inconsistent grounding across frames, brittle editing and a native resolution capped at 672 by 384. No outside benchmarks exist yet.

stories.headline: T3 Code lets coding agents draw live visualizations inside the chat thread
stories.standfirst: Theo's T3 Code now lets agents build dynamic visualizations inside a thread, styled with the user's own theme. The maker's clip drew 969 likes in about an hour.
body: T3 Code, the open-source app that lets developers run coding agents from one window, says it has shipped in-app visualization. Theo, its developer, said on X the feature "enables agents to build cool dynamic experiences within the thread". His post carries a short video and had 969 likes when read at around 02:00 UTC on 6 October, about an hour after he posted it.

Theo credited a contributor known as davis7 with pushing for the feature and building most of it. He said he "didn't expect to dig it so much". The post gives no list of what kinds of visualization are supported, and the video is the only demonstration of it so far. Nobody outside the team has publicly tested the feature.

In a reply, Theo said the agent is handed CSS style tokens from the theme the user has chosen, so a visualization should always match the app. Whether that holds is untested. In a second post he called theme compatibility "the coolest part". Both statements are the maker's own, and neither says how well the match holds across custom themes.

T3 Code describes itself on GitHub as an agent harness control surface that works with providers including Claude Code and Codex, across desktop, web and phone apps. The repository is MIT-licensed and showed 25.6k stars when read. Its README warns the project is "very very early" and says users should expect bugs, so the feature may be rough.

stories.headline: Anthropic staff gave $540m in 2025, five times the next corporate donor
stories.standfirst: The Information reports IPO documents show Anthropic employees donated $540 million in 2025, helped by a share top-up program. The next biggest Fortune 500 donors gave about $115 million.
body: Anthropic employees donated $540 million in 2025, nearly five times as much as the next-largest Fortune 500 donors, The Information reported, according to a summary by The Decoder on 5 October. The figures come from company documents shared with prospective IPO investors. Anthropic has not published them, and neither The Decoder nor this paper has seen the documents.

The report says staff gave a further $660 million between October 2025 and March 2026. For comparison, the Decoder says Truist Financial gave $115 million and BlackRock $109 million, the closest Fortune 500 totals it cites. The comparison is between employee donations and corporate giving, so the two groups are not strictly like for like.

The size comes from a company program. Employees donate shares to charities, and Anthropic tops up each gift with extra shares. According to the report, early employees get a triple match on the value of their donation, while the match rate for others varies with how long they have been at the company.

The Decoder says the top-ups dilute other shareholders, and that totals could reach billions after an IPO if the stock rises. It adds that CEO Dario Amodei and six co-founders have pledged to give away at least 80 percent of their wealth. Anthropic has not commented in the coverage read, and no second outlet has confirmed the numbers.

stories.headline: Researchers track an AI 'agent fleet' asking Amap for zoo directions
stories.standfirst: Researchers say many parallel AI agents, apparently on Tencent servers, query Alibaba's Amap for routes to a park, a zoo and a hospital. They see no sign the agents talk.
body: Independent researchers have found what they call an "agent fleet" that appears to run on Tencent's infrastructure and target Alibaba's Amap map service, TechCrunch reported on 5 October. They spotted it in traffic logs from urlquery, a domain-scanning service. The report names no owner or purpose, and no other outlet had confirmed the findings when this was written.

According to TechCrunch, the agents ask Amap for directions to different entrances of public places, including a park, a zoo and a hospital. One researcher distinguished a fleet from a swarm: "many parallel agents on the same kind of task, with no sign of communication between them." That, the researchers argue, is what separates this from coordinated multi-agent behaviour.

The agents made little effort to hide, TechCrunch says, and left records in the scanning logs. The report ties the find to tighter monitoring for rogue agents since the Hugging Face incident. Researchers caution the activity may be benign compared with what could come.

What the agents are for is unknown. The observed queries are routine map lookups. TechCrunch does not say who runs the fleet or how large it is, or whether Tencent or Alibaba has commented. Until the operator or a vendor responds, the account rests on the researchers' reading of the logs.

stories.headline: Etched is reported to be fielding funding offers at a $40bn to $50bn valuation
stories.standfirst: TechCrunch, citing sources, says the inference-chip start-up is in early talks at $40 billion to $50 billion, up from $21 billion last month. Etched says it has $1 billion in customer orders.
body: Etched, the AI inference-chip start-up, is fielding funding offers at a valuation between $40 billion and $50 billion, TechCrunch reported on 5 October, citing sources. The talks are early and nothing has closed. No other outlet had confirmed the figures when this was written, and Etched had not publicly commented on the valuation.

The offers would roughly double the $21 billion valuation from its last round, a $700 million raise in September that TechCrunch says Jane Street led. Jane Street is also a customer. In July, TechCrunch reports, Etched raised $300 million at $10.3 billion in a round led by Sequoia, so its price has risen fourfold in three months.

Etched designs chips meant to speed up inference, with faster token processing and lower costs than Nvidia's, according to the report. Co-founder and chief operating officer Robert Wachen is quoted saying investors are keen because the company "designed two new components from scratch to speed up inference." Those performance claims are the company's and unverified here.

TechCrunch says the company has about 400 staff, roughly 15 percent from Nvidia, and has secured $1 billion in customer orders. It runs a 10-megawatt data centre in Silicon Valley and a Taiwan facility near TSMC. The founders, Gavin Uberti, Chris Zhu and Wachen, started the company about four years ago.
